name: Acne
description: Acne is a common skin condition that occurs when hair follicles become blocked with oil and dead skin cells, leading to spots and inflammation, most often on the face, chest and back.
symptoms: blackheads
whiteheads
papules
pustules
oily skin
tenderness or soreness of affected areas
scarring or dark marks after spots heal
causes: excess sebum production
blocked hair follicles
Cutibacterium acnes bacteria
hormonal changes such as puberty, menstruation or pregnancy
genetic predisposition
certain medications and cosmetic products
treatments: gentle skin cleansing routines
over-the-counter topical treatments such as benzoyl peroxide or salicylic acid
prescription topical retinoids
topical or oral antibiotics prescribed by a clinician
hormonal treatments in some cases
oral isotretinoin for severe cases under specialist supervision
avoiding picking or squeezing spots to reduce scarring
when_to_seek_help: Consider seeing a pharmacist or doctor if acne is moderate to severe, painful, leaving scars or dark marks, not improving after several weeks of over-the-counter treatment, or causing significant distress. Only a healthcare professional can confirm the diagnosis and recommend suitable treatment.

name: Actinic Keratosis
description: Actinic keratosis is a rough, scaly patch of skin caused by long-term ultraviolet light exposure. It is considered a pre-cancerous change because a small proportion of lesions can progress to squamous cell carcinoma, so professional assessment is important.
symptoms: rough, dry or scaly patches of skin
patches that are flat or slightly raised
pink, red, brown or skin-coloured lesions
patches commonly on the face, scalp, ears, neck, forearms or backs of hands
itching, burning or tenderness in the affected area
patches that come and go or slowly enlarge
causes: cumulative ultraviolet exposure from sunlight
use of sunbeds or tanning devices
fair skin that burns easily
older age
a weakened immune system, including after organ transplantation
outdoor work or extensive outdoor recreation
previous history of sun damage or skin cancer
treatments: medical assessment to confirm the diagnosis and exclude skin cancer
cryotherapy (freezing) performed by a clinician
prescription topical treatments such as 5-fluorouracil, imiquimod or diclofenac gel
photodynamic therapy
curettage or shave excision with or without biopsy
ongoing sun protection with high-factor sunscreen, clothing and shade
regular skin monitoring and clinical follow-up
when_to_seek_help: Actinic keratosis should be assessed by a doctor or dermatologist, as it can look similar to skin cancer and cannot be diagnosed reliably from appearance or symptoms alone. Seek prompt medical advice if a patch grows, thickens, bleeds, ulcerates, becomes painful or changes in appearance.

name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
description: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer, arising from basal cells in the outer layer of the skin. It usually grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body, but it can damage surrounding tissue if untreated, so medical diagnosis and treatment are essential.
symptoms: a pearly, waxy or translucent bump
a flat, scaly patch that may be pink, red or brown
a sore or spot that bleeds, crusts and does not heal
visible small blood vessels on the surface of the lesion
a lesion with a raised, rolled edge and a central depression or ulcer
itching or occasional bleeding from the area
lesions most often on sun-exposed skin such as the face, head, neck or shoulders
causes: long-term or intense ultraviolet exposure from sunlight
use of sunbeds or tanning devices
fair skin, light eyes or skin that burns easily
increasing age
a personal or family history of skin cancer
a weakened immune system or immunosuppressive medication
previous radiotherapy or exposure to arsenic
certain inherited conditions such as basal cell naevus syndrome
treatments: clinical examination and skin biopsy to confirm the diagnosis
surgical excision
Mohs micrographic surgery for high-risk or facial lesions
curettage and cautery
cryotherapy for selected superficial lesions
prescription topical therapies such as imiquimod or 5-fluorouracil for some superficial types
photodynamic therapy
radiotherapy when surgery is unsuitable
targeted drug therapy for advanced disease
long-term sun protection and regular skin checks
when_to_seek_help: Any new, changing, bleeding or non-healing skin lesion should be assessed by a doctor without delay, as basal cell carcinoma cannot be diagnosed from symptoms or appearance alone and requires professional examination, often with a biopsy. Early diagnosis and treatment usually give the best outcome and reduce the risk of tissue damage or scarring.

name: Rosacea
description: Rosacea is a long-term inflammatory skin condition that mainly affects the central face, causing persistent redness, flushing and sometimes spots or visible blood vessels. It tends to follow a pattern of flare-ups and quieter periods.
symptoms: persistent facial redness, especially on the cheeks, nose, chin and forehead
episodes of flushing or blushing
visible small blood vessels (telangiectasia)
papules and pustules resembling acne
burning, stinging or sensitive skin
dry, rough or swollen skin
eye irritation, dryness or grittiness in ocular rosacea
thickened skin of the nose (rhinophyma) in some long-standing cases
causes: not fully understood, but thought to involve abnormal immune and inflammatory responses
abnormalities in facial blood vessels and nerve signalling
genetic predisposition and family history
Demodex mites and skin microbe changes
common triggers including sunlight, heat, cold wind, spicy food, alcohol, hot drinks, exercise and stress
some skincare products and medications, including topical steroids
treatments: identifying and avoiding personal triggers
gentle, non-irritating skincare and daily sun protection
prescription topical treatments such as metronidazole, azelaic acid or ivermectin
topical brimonidine to reduce redness
oral antibiotics such as doxycycline for inflammatory papules and pustules
oral isotretinoin in resistant cases under specialist supervision
laser or light-based treatment for visible blood vessels and persistent redness
eye lubricants or specialist referral for ocular involvement
when_to_seek_help: See a doctor or pharmacist if facial redness or spots are persistent, worsening or affecting your confidence, and seek medical advice promptly if your eyes become sore, red or affected, or if the skin on your nose begins to thicken. A healthcare professional is needed to confirm the diagnosis, as rosacea can resemble other skin conditions.
